lessons.title: который: the case comes from inside the clause, and the preposition comes with it
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 73 gave you который (ka-TO-ryy, 'who, which, that') as a reading signal: when a clause opens with it, the clause is describing the noun in front. This lesson turns that recognition into production, and production forces a decision that reading never forces, because you must choose the case of который before you open your mouth. The rule itself has not changed. Cornell states it in one line: который agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case depends on its function in its own clause. What changes is the order in which you apply it. A reader sees the ending and works backwards; a speaker starts from the meaning and has to arrive at the ending.

Take the masculine noun человек (chee-la-VYEK, 'person, man') and run it through all six cases inside a relative clause. Nominative, when the person is the one doing the action: человек, который работает здесь (chee-la-VYEK, ka-TO-ryy ra-BO-ta-yet zdyes, 'the man who works here'). Genitive, when the clause needs the person as a starting point or as a possessor: человек, у которого нет времени (oo ka-TO-ra-va nyet VRYE-mee-nee, 'the man who has no time', literally 'at whom there is no time'). Dative, when the person is the recipient or the person called: человек, которому я позвонил (ka-TO-ra-moo ya paz-va-NEEL, 'the man I called'). Accusative, when the person is the direct object: человек, которого я видел (ka-TO-ra-va ya VEE-deel, 'the man I saw'). Instrumental, when the person is a companion or an instrument: человек, с которым я работал (s ka-TO-rym ya ra-BO-tal, 'the man I worked with'). Prepositional, when the person is the topic: человек, о котором мы говорили (a ka-TO-ram my ga-va-REE-lee, 'the man we were talking about'). Six sentences, one noun, six endings, and the noun's gender and number never moved.

The gender agreement is what makes the word look like an adjective, and the case is what makes it behave like a pronoun. книга, которая лежит на столе (KNEE-ga, ka-TO-ra-ya lee-ZHEET na sta-LYE, 'the book that is lying on the table') shows the feminine, письмо, которое пришло вчера (pees-MO, ka-TO-ra-ye preesh-LO fchee-RA, 'the letter that arrived yesterday') shows the neuter, and книги, которые лежат на столе (KNEE-gee, ka-TO-ry-ye lee-ZHAT na sta-LYE, 'the books that are lying on the table') shows the plural. The pattern is regular enough to trust: который declines exactly like an ordinary adjective of the hard stem, so any adjective table you already know gives you the form.

Prepositions are the part that English speakers lose. English moves the relative word to the front of its clause and leaves the preposition behind, which is why 'the house I live in' is normal English. Russian cannot do that. The preposition belongs to its case, and the case belongs to который, so the two travel together and stand at the head of the clause: дом, в котором мы живём (DOM, f ka-TO-ram my zhee-VYOM, 'the house we live in'). alphaDictionary makes the contrast explicit on its page for который: English leaves the preposition in its original position, and Russian does not allow it. So the phrase 'the house which we live in' has exactly one Russian shape, and the shape is not word-for-word.

'Whose' needs its own note because English has a single word and Russian has three routes. The ordinary spoken route is у которого, literally 'at whom': коллега, у которого я учился (ka-LEE-ga, oo ka-TO-ra-va ya oo-CHEEL-sya, 'the colleague I learned the job from'). The written route puts the possessed thing in the genitive and который agrees with it: дом, окна которого выходят на юг (DOM, OK-na ka-TO-ra-va VY-kho-dyat na YOOK, 'the house whose windows face south'). The literary route is чей (chyey, 'whose'), which declines like a possessive: писатель, чьи книги мы читаем (pee-SA-teel, chyee KNEE-gee my chee-TA-yem, 'the writer whose books we read'). Choose у которого in speech, the genitive in reports, and чей only when you are deliberately writing in a bookish key.

One punctuation fact separates Russian from English. English uses commas to distinguish a clause that identifies its noun from one that merely adds information. Russian sets off every который clause with commas, so the distinction is carried by intonation and context rather than by the comma. That is convenient when you write and dangerous when you read aloud, because a long identifying clause still gets a pause that English would not give it.
lessons.example:
Build one clause four times from the same pair of sentences, changing only the job the woman does in the second clause. Start with the frame: Я знаю женщину (ya ZNA-yoo ZHEN-shee-noo, 'I know the woman'). Now add the information. She works here: Я знаю женщину, которая работает здесь (ka-TO-ra-ya ra-BO-ta-yet zdyes). I see her every day: Я знаю женщину, которую я вижу каждый день (ka-TO-roo-yoo ya VEE-zhoo KAZH-dyy dyen). She has no time: Я знаю женщину, у которой нет времени (oo ka-TO-ray nyet VRYE-mee-nee). I spoke with her: Я знаю женщину, с которой я говорил (s ka-TO-ray ya ga-va-REEL). Four clauses, one antecedent, and the only thing that changed is the ending on который, because the only thing that changed is the woman's role inside the second clause.

Now do the same in writing, where the clauses can stack. Мы приняли проект, который подготовила комиссия (my pree-NYA-lee pra-YEKT, ka-TO-ryy pad-ga-TO-vee-la ka-MEE-see-ya, 'we accepted the project that the commission prepared'). Комиссия, в которую входят пять специалистов, работала два месяца (ka-MEE-see-ya, f ka-TO-roo-yoo FKHO-dyat PYAT spet-see-a-LEE-staf, ra-BO-ta-la dva MYE-sya-tsa, 'the commission, which includes five specialists, worked for two months'). Решение, о котором мы говорим, вступит в силу в январе (ree-SHYE-nee-ye, a ka-TO-ram my ga-va-REEM, fstoo-PEET f SEE-loo f yeen-va-RYE, 'the decision we are discussing comes into force in January'). Three clauses, three different cases, all governed from inside their own clause: nominative because the commission is the subject of подготовила, accusative because the specialists enter the commission, prepositional because the decision is the topic of говорим.

Test every one of them by removing который and putting the noun back in its place. Комиссия подготовила проект gives you the nominative source of который. В комиссию входят пять специалистов gives you the accusative, with the preposition в in front. Мы говорим о решении gives you the prepositional, with о in front. If the restored sentence is grammatical, the relative clause is grammatical; if you cannot restore it, you have guessed the case rather than chosen it.
lessons.question: You want to say 'the colleague I share an office with' and produce «коллега, который я работаю в одном кабинете». What has gone wrong, and what should you say?
lessons.answer: который has been left in the nominative because English 'who' shows no case; the colleague is the person you work with, so the clause needs the instrumental with its preposition: «коллега, с которым я работаю в одном кабинете».
lessons.distractor: The sentence is correct, because который always agrees with коллега and коллега is masculine singular, so the masculine singular form is right.
lessons.correction: Agreement in gender and number is only half of the rule, and the half that is easy to see. The other half is case, and case is decided inside the clause: работать с кем, 'to work with someone', takes the instrumental, so the relative word is которым and the preposition с must stand immediately in front of it. The distracter describes the mistake exactly, because it treats the agreement with коллега as the whole requirement. English 'who' and Spanish 'que' both hide case, and Spanish even keeps the preposition in front (con el que), which is the one habit worth transferring. Say коллега, с которым я работаю (ka-LEE-ga, s ka-TO-rym ya ra-BO-ta-yoo) and the clause is both grammatical and speakable.

depth.definitions: The antecedent is the noun outside the clause that the clause describes, here коллега. The relative pronoun is the word that opens the clause and stands in for that noun, here который. Agreement is the copying of gender and number from the antecedent onto the pronoun, which is why the pronoun looks like an adjective. Case government is the requirement that a preposition or a verb imposes a particular case on the word it controls: с imposes the instrumental, у imposes the genitive, о imposes the prepositional. Stranding is the English habit of leaving a preposition at the end of a clause when its object has moved to the front, as in 'the house I live in'; Russian has no stranding, so the preposition moves with its object. A restrictive clause identifies which noun you mean, a non-restrictive clause adds a comment about a noun already identified; English separates them with commas, Russian does not.
depth.mechanism:
The production algorithm has three steps and you should say them in order until they are automatic. First, name the antecedent and record its gender and number, because that half of the ending is already decided. Second, say the second clause on its own with the noun in place, and listen to what the verb or the preposition demands: я работаю с коллегой gives you the instrumental, у коллеги нет времени gives you the genitive, я говорю о коллеге gives you the prepositional. Third, delete the noun, put который in the case you just heard, and move any preposition to the front with it.

The animacy rule sits inside step three and only affects the accusative. If the antecedent is animate and masculine, the accusative of который is которого, identical to the genitive; if it is inanimate, the accusative is который, identical to the nominative. That is why человек, которого я видел has a genitive-looking form with an accusative job, and проект, который я видел keeps the nominative-looking form. Feminine and neuter forms do not distinguish animacy in the accusative, which is why книга, которую я читаю is unambiguous.

Prepositions that govern unusual cases are worth drilling because they expose the mechanism. мимо которого (MEE-ma ka-TO-ra-va, 'past which') takes the genitive and cannot be replaced by a nominative form. благодаря которому (bla-ga-da-RYA ka-TO-ra-moo, 'thanks to which') takes the dative. между которыми (MYEZH-doo ka-TO-ry-mee, 'between which') takes the instrumental plural. None of these can be guessed from the antecedent, and all of them become easy once you restore the noun and let the preposition tell you the case.
depth.secondExample:
Take a written paragraph about a decision and watch the relative word change case three times without changing its gender. Суд принял решение, которое обжаловала компания (soot pree-NYAL ree-SHYE-nee-ye, ka-TO-ra-ye ab-ZHA-la-va-la kam-PA-nee-ya, 'the court took a decision that the company appealed'). The decision is neuter singular, and inside its clause it is the object of обжаловала, so the form is the accusative neuter, which happens to look like the nominative. Теперь мы читаем документ, в котором изложены причины отказа (tee-PYER my chee-TA-yem da-koo-MENT, f ka-TO-ram eez-LO-zhe-ny pree-CHEE-ny at-KA-za, 'now we are reading the document that sets out the grounds for refusal'). Here the antecedent is document, masculine, and the clause puts it inside в, so the form is the prepositional. Наконец, есть юрист, с которым мы советуемся каждый вторник (na-ka-NYETS, yest yoo-REEST, s ka-TO-rym my sa-VYE-too-yem-sya KAZH-dyy FTOR-neek, 'finally, there is a lawyer we consult every Tuesday'). Masculine again, but the verb советоваться requires с plus the instrumental.

Now read the three relative words in sequence: которое, котором, которым. The gender shifted once, at the second clause, and the case shifted twice. If you can explain each shift by restoring the noun into its clause, you own the pattern. If you cannot, the ending was copied from the previous clause, which is the most common production error after the nominative default.
depth.mistake:
Three errors recur. The first is the stranded preposition: a learner says дом, который мы живём в, translating English word for word. The repair is mechanical, because the preposition must be pulled forward and the case recomputed: дом, в котором мы живём. The second is the nominative default: every который comes out as который because English 'who' and 'that' never change, and Spanish 'que' never changes either. The repair is the restore test from the mechanism section, said aloud before the relative clause is spoken. The third is the 'whose' calque: a learner writes которого работа or чей работа, mixing the two systems. The spoken repair is to rebuild with у: человек, у которого интересная работа (chee-la-VYEK, oo ka-TO-ra-va in-tee-RYES-na-ya ra-BO-ta, 'a man whose job is interesting').

A subtler error belongs to Spanish and Italian speakers who have learned that the preposition goes first, and then over-apply it to the genitive of possession. They produce дом, в которого окна, because they feel a preposition is needed. The written possessive genitive takes no preposition at all: дом, окна которого. The test is whether the noun after который is the possessed thing; if it is, который is genitive and stands alone.
depth.application:
Take five true pairs of sentences about your own work and join each pair twice, once in speech and once in a written register. For example: Я работаю в отделе. Отдел занимается закупками. (ya ra-BO-ta-yoo v at-DYE-lee. at-DYEL za-nee-MA-yet-sya za-KOOP-ka-mee, 'I work in a department. The department handles purchasing.') Join as Я работаю в отделе, который занимается закупками (f at-DYE-le, ka-TO-ryy za-nee-MA-yet-sya za-KOOP-ka-mee). Then a pair that needs the genitive: У меня есть начальник. У начальника двадцать лет опыта. (oo mee-NYA yest na-CHAL-neek. oo na-CHAL-nee-ka DVAT-tsat lyet O-py-ta, 'I have a boss. The boss has twenty years of experience.') Join as У меня есть начальник, у которого двадцать лет опыта (oo ka-TO-ra-va DVAT-tsat lyet O-py-ta). Then a pair that needs the dative: Есть коллега. Я помогаю коллеге. (yest ka-LEE-ga. ya pa-ma-GA-yoo ka-LEE-gee, 'there is a colleague. I help the colleague.') Join as Есть коллега, которому я помогаю (ka-TO-ra-moo ya pa-ma-GA-yoo).

Say each joined sentence aloud twice, once slowly with the restore step spoken first, once at speed. Then write the same five sentences in a paragraph and check every relative word against its own clause, not against the noun in front. If a sentence contains two который clauses, check them separately, because a long sentence lets the second ending drift toward the first.
depth.summary: который copies gender and number from the noun it describes and takes its case from the job it does inside its own clause. Prepositions travel with it and stand in front, because Russian does not strand prepositions at the end. 'Whose' is у которого in speech, the genitive of который in writing, and чей in a deliberately literary register. Build the clause by restoring the noun first, then deleting it, and the ending will be right the first time.

This is the page that states the contrast this lesson needs: English moves the relative word to the front and leaves the preposition behind, Russian cannot, so the preposition must be fronted with the pronoun. It also makes the point that Russian allows neither что nor omission in place of который after a concrete noun, which is why English 'the man I met' has only one Russian shape. visual.title: Six-case ladder for один antecedent
visual.description: A labelled text diagram: one noun written at the top, six rungs below it, each rung holding the relative word in one case, the clause it belongs to, and the restored sentence that proves the case. Rendered as text steps, not as an image.
steps: Step 1, fix the top of the ladder. Write ЧЕЛОВЕК in capitals and beside it the labels 'masculine, singular, animate'. Every rung below must show a masculine singular form; that part never changes, which is the point of putting it at the top.

Step 2, fill the six rungs in case order. Nominative который, genitive которого, dative которому, accusative которого, instrumental которым, prepositional котором. Beside each form write the preposition that belongs to it, if any: у, none, none, с, о.

Step 3, write the restored sentence on every rung. For the instrumental rung, я работаю с человеком; for the prepositional rung, мы говорим о человеке. The restored sentence is the evidence for the form, and a rung without evidence is a guess.

Step 4, add the feminine column. Write КНИГА beside ЧЕЛОВЕК and fill the same six rungs with которая, которой, которой, которую, которой, которой. Mark the accusative rung, because it is the one form that visibly differs from the masculine and therefore the one that proves agreement is real.

Step 5, mark the preposition rule. Draw an arrow from each preposition to the relative word on its rung and write 'no stranding' beside the arrow. This is the only rung where an English sentence would put the preposition somewhere else.

lessons.title: что and чтобы: a fact, a purpose, and a wish are three different clauses
lessons.explanation:
Two words that differ by one letter do two completely different jobs, and the difference is not stylistic. что (SHTO, 'that') introduces a clause that reports something as a fact, something the speaker presents as true or false. чтобы (SHTO-by, 'so that, in order to') introduces a clause that is not asserted at all: a purpose, a wish, an order, a requirement. Lesson 76 established that Russian does not shift tense in reported speech, so the clause after что keeps the tense the original speaker used. This lesson adds the other half of the system, the half that decides whether you report a fact or impose a wish.

Cornell prints the minimal pair that makes the contrast visible. Она сказала, что они подписали письмо (a-NA ska-ZA-la, SHTO a-NEE pad-PEE-sa-lee pees-MO, 'she said that they had signed the letter') reports a fact about the past. Она сказала, чтобы они подписали письмо (a-NA ska-ZA-la, SHTO-by a-NEE pad-PEE-sa-lee pees-MO, 'she told them to sign the letter') issues an instruction. The words after the conjunction are identical, including the past-tense form подписали, and the sentences mean different things because the conjunction changed the speech act. That is the whole lesson in one pair: что reports, чтобы directs.

The clearest proof that чтобы is not about past time is a sentence with a future adverb. Я хочу, чтобы он пришёл завтра (ya kha-CHOO, SHTO-by on pree-SHYOL ZAF-tra, 'I want him to come tomorrow') contains a past-tense form and refers to tomorrow. The form пришёл is not past tense in meaning here; it is the shape that чтобы requires, and the time comes from the adverb or from the context. Learners who translate the form as past tense produce 'I want that he came yesterday', which is why the grammar has to be learned as a pattern rather than translated word for word.

The same-subject rule decides between an infinitive and a full clause, and Cornell states it as a warning. If the two verbs share one subject, use an infinitive: Я хочу петь (ya kha-CHOO PYET, 'I want to sing'), where the person who wants and the person who sings are the same. If the subjects differ, use чтобы plus the past form: Я хочу, чтобы он пел (ya kha-CHOO, SHTO-by on PYEL, 'I want him to sing'). English uses an infinitive in both sentences, 'I want to sing' and 'I want him to sing', so the English speaker has no signal that Russian changes construction. Spanish is more helpful here, because querer que takes a subjunctive clause and thus marks the different subject overtly.

Purpose is the third use, and it follows the same subject rule. With one subject, чтобы plus the infinitive means 'in order to': Я купил учебник, чтобы заниматься русским языком (ya koo-PEEL oo-CHEB-neek, SHTO-by za-nee-MAT-sya ROOS-keem yee-zy-KOM, 'I bought a textbook in order to study Russian'). With two subjects, the past form returns: Я говорю тихо, чтобы не разбудить ребёнка (ya ga-va-RYU TEE-kha, SHTO-by ne raz-boo-DEET ree-BYON-ka, 'I speak quietly so as not to wake the child'), where the negative purpose is чтобы не and the subject is still shared, so the infinitive stays.

A fourth use is easy to miss because it looks like a relative clause. After всё, то and тот, что is the relative word, not a conjunction: всё, что он сказал (VSYO, SHTO on ska-ZAL, 'everything he said'), то, что мы видели (TO, SHTO my VEE-dee-lee, 'what we saw'). The demonstrative sets up a slot and что fills it. This is why то, что can open a sentence and take a comma after the clause: То, что он сказал, было правдой (TO, SHTO on ska-ZAL, BY-la PRAF-day, 'what he said was true').
lessons.example:
Run one workplace situation through all four constructions and listen to what each one does. The fact: Начальник сказал, что проект готов (na-CHAL-neek ska-ZAL, SHTO pra-YEKT ga-TOF, 'the boss said the project is ready'). The instruction: Начальник сказал, чтобы мы проверили смету (SHTO-by my pra-VYE-ree-lee SMYE-too, 'the boss told us to check the estimate'). The purpose with a shared subject: Мы остались, чтобы проверить цифры (my as-TA-lee-sya, SHTO-by pra-VYE-reet TSEEF-ry, 'we stayed in order to check the figures'). The wish with two subjects: Я хотел, чтобы он подписал документ сегодня (ya kha-TYEL, SHTO-by on pad-pee-SAL da-koo-MENT see-VO-dnya, 'I wanted him to sign the document today').

Now read the four conjunctions in order: что, чтобы, чтобы, чтобы. Only the first reports. The second and third direct or intend, and the difference between them is whether the person who checks is the person who stayed. The fourth is a wish about someone else, and its past form подписал refers to a signature that may not exist yet, which is the point that surprises learners most.

Finally the relative use, in a sentence a manager might write. Важно, чтобы все поняли, что от них требуется (VAZH-na, SHTO-by fsye PO-nya-lee, SHTO at neekh TRYE-boo-yet-sya, 'it is important that everyone understands what is required of them'). Two conjunctions in one sentence, and they are doing different work: чтобы introduces the requirement, что introduces the content that must be understood. A learner who uses чтобы twice produces a sentence that sounds as if the requirement were still being negotiated.
lessons.question: You want to say 'I want you to read this document before the meeting' and produce «Я хочу, что вы прочитали этот документ до встречи». What is wrong, and what should it be?
lessons.answer: The wish has two subjects, I want and you read, so it needs чтобы plus the past form: «Я хочу, чтобы вы прочитали этот документ до встречи».
lessons.distractor: The sentence is correct, because что introduces the content of what I want, and the past form прочитали marks the action as complete.
lessons.correction: что reports a fact and cannot report a wish. The moment the main verb expresses a want, a request, a requirement or an instruction, the conjunction is чтобы, and the dependent verb takes the past form even when the action lies in the future. Hence Я хочу, чтобы вы прочитали (ya kha-CHOO, SHTO-by vy pra-chee-TA-lee). The distracter is a real stage in learning, because the learner has understood that the content clause needs a conjunction and has not yet learned that Russian splits content into fact and non-fact. English 'I want that you read' is not English, but it is the shape the translation produces, and Spanish querer que would have pushed the learner toward a subjunctive clause, which Russian marks with чтобы.

depth.definitions: A factive predicate treats its clause as a claim about the world: сказать, сообщить, знать, думать, помнить, надеяться, бояться, plus impersonal predicates such as известно, ясно, правда. A non-factive predicate treats its clause as something wanted, ordered or needed rather than asserted: хотеть, просить, советовать, требовать, нужно, важно, нельзя. A complement clause is the clause that completes such a predicate. A purpose clause gives the intended result of an action. Same-subject means one person does both verbs, different-subject means two. The correlative то, что is a demonstrative plus a relative word, not a conjunction, and it means 'the thing that'.
depth.mechanism:
Operate the choice as a two-question test, in this order. First question: does the clause claim that something is or was the case? If yes, use что and keep the tense that the meaning requires, because Russian has no sequence-of-tense rule to apply. Second question: if the clause is not a claim, is it a purpose or a wish? For a purpose, use чтобы: with an infinitive if the subjects match, with the past form if they do not. For a wish, an order or a requirement, use чтобы plus the past form, and let adverbs or context supply the time.

The subject test is the one that decides the infinitive, and it is worth running aloud. Say the main verb with its subject, then say the second verb with the subject you intend. If the two subjects are the same person, the second verb goes into the infinitive. Я хочу поехать and Я хочу, чтобы он поехал are both correct, and the only difference is who travels. The same test gives Я купил учебник, чтобы заниматься and Я купил учебник, чтобы сын занимался.

Two mechanical consequences follow. чтобы is never followed by a present-tense form; the form after чтобы is either an infinitive or a past-tense form, with no third option. And что is never followed by an infinitive, because an infinitive does not assert anything: Я надеюсь приехать has no conjunction at all, while Я надеюсь, что он приедет needs one. When you find yourself wanting to put an infinitive after что, the sentence usually wants no conjunction or wants чтобы.
depth.secondExample:
Read a short instruction from a manager and label every clause before translating. Я прошу, чтобы вы подготовили отчёт к пятнице (ya pra-SHOO, SHTO-by vy pad-ga-TO-vee-lee at-CHYOT k PYAT-nee-tse, 'I ask that you prepare the report by Friday'). The first clause is a request, so чтобы and the past form подготовили, even though Friday has not arrived. Важно, чтобы цифры были точными (VAZH-na, SHTO-by TSEEF-ry BY-lee TOCH-ny-mee, 'it is important that the figures be accurate'). An impersonal predicate of necessity, so чтобы again, and the past form были carries no past meaning at all. Я уверен, что вы справитесь (ya oo-VYE-ren, SHTO pra-VEE-tees, 'I am sure you will manage'). A factive predicate, so что, and the future tense stays future because Russian does not backshift.

Now compare the second and third sentences. Both express the speaker's attitude, and only one of them asserts anything about the world. Важно, чтобы is a requirement, and the figures may or may not be accurate; я уверен, что is a belief, and the speaker is committed to the proposition. The conjunction is the visible marker of that difference, which is why a report that mixes them reads as either hesitant or overconfident.
depth.mistake:
The classic error is 'I want that he came', the literal translation of a wish with что. It happens because English and Spanish both use a complement clause after 'want' and 'querer', and only the mood, which Russian lacks in this construction, marks the difference. The repair is to memorise three verbs that always take чтобы, хотеть, просить, требовать, and the impersonal three, нужно, важно, нельзя, and to say the pattern with a past form until it sounds normal.

The second error is the reverse: using чтобы to report a fact, as in Он сказал, чтобы проект готов, where the speaker means 'he said the project is ready'. The repair is to ask whether anyone is being told to do something. If nobody is, the conjunction is что.

The third error is a spelling confusion that changes the meaning. чтобы is one word and introduces a subordinate clause. что бы is two words, the conditional что plus the particle бы: Что бы ты сделал? (SHTO by ty SDYE-lal, 'what would you do?'). The test is whether бы can move or be replaced: in что бы ты сделал, бы belongs to the verb and the phrase means 'what would', so the two words stay separate. This is the same бы from lesson 104, and it keeps its independence.
depth.application:
Take six sentences about your own week and say each one twice, once as a fact and once as a wish or instruction, changing only the conjunction and the verb form. Model: Он сказал, что отчёт готов. Он сказал, чтобы отчёт был готов к утру. (on ska-ZAL, SHTO at-CHYOT ga-TOF. on ska-ZAL, SHTO-by at-CHYOT byl ga-TOF k oot-ROO, 'he said the report is ready. He said the report should be ready by morning.') Model: Я знаю, что она придёт. Я хочу, чтобы она пришла. (ya ZNA-yoo, SHTO a-NA pree-DYOT. ya kha-CHOO, SHTO-by a-NA preesh-LA, 'I know she will come. I want her to come.') Model: Мы уверены, что цифры верные. Нужно, чтобы цифры были верными. (my oo-VYE-re-ny, SHTO TSEEF-ry VYER-ny-ye. NOOZH-na, SHTO-by TSEEF-ry BY-lee VYER-ny-mee, 'we are sure the figures are right. It is necessary that the figures be right.')

Then write a short email with four sentences: one fact, one requirement, one purpose with a shared subject, one purpose with a different subject. Read it aloud and stop at every conjunction to say which test it passed. If a sentence contains both что and чтобы, as the manager's sentence did, check them in the order they appear, because the first one sets the frame for the second.
depth.summary: что reports a fact and keeps the tense the meaning needs; чтобы introduces a purpose, a wish, an order or a requirement and never takes a present-tense form. One subject takes an infinitive, two subjects take the past form. After всё and то, что is a relative word rather than a conjunction, which is why то, что can open a sentence. The test is always the same: is anything being asserted, or is something being wanted?

lessons.title: Conditions: если for what may happen, если бы for what did not
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 104 introduced бы as the marker of the unreal and showed that it combines with a past-tense form. This lesson builds the two-clause architecture around it and sets it against the real conditional, because the choice between the two is the first decision a speaker makes and the rest of the sentence follows from it. The real conditional uses если (YEs-lee, 'if') with ordinary indicative verbs, and the tense in each clause is whatever the meaning requires. The unreal conditional uses если бы (YEs-lee by, 'if') with a past-tense form in both clauses, and that one shape covers present, past and future alike.

Start with the real conditional, which has three common shapes. A general truth puts the present in both clauses, or an infinitive in the если-clause: Если нагреть воду до ста градусов, она закипает (YEs-lee na-GRYET va-DOO da STA GRA-doo-saf, a-NA za-kee-PA-yet, 'if you heat water to a hundred degrees, it boils'). A prediction about the future puts a perfective future in the если-clause and a future or an imperative in the main clause: Если ты позвонишь, я отвечу (YEs-lee ty paz-va-NEESH, ya at-VYE-choo, 'if you call, I will answer'), and Если увидишь его, скажи мне (YEs-lee oo-VEE-deesh ye-VO, ska-ZHEE mnye, 'if you see him, tell me'). A condition about the past puts the past in both clauses: Если он пришёл, значит, он согласен (YEs-lee on pree-SHYOL, ZNA-cheet, on sag-LA-sen, 'if he came, then he agrees').

English speakers have to be told that если takes the future tense quite happily. 'If I will' is not English, so the learner avoids позвонишь and produces Если ты будешь звонить, which shifts the aspect and suggests a process rather than a single call. The rule is that the если-clause names a completed event in the future with a perfective verb, and the main clause names the consequence. Aspect, not tense, carries the difference between a single completed condition and a repeated or ongoing one, which is the same aspect logic from lesson 58 applied inside a conditional.

The unreal conditional is simpler in form and harder in habit. Cornell puts the form rule plainly: use бы plus the past-tense form in both clauses, and since there is no choice of forms you do not have to worry about past, present or future, or about the difference between a hypothesis and a counterfactual. One sentence covers them all: Если бы он пришёл, мы бы поехали за город (YEs-lee by on pree-SHYOL, my by pa-YE-ha-lee ZA ga-rat). Out of context that means 'if he came, we would go to the country', 'if he had come, we would have gone', or 'if he were to come, we would go'. Context and adverbs decide the time, and the forms never change.

The habit that fails is the single бы. English puts 'would' only in the main clause, so the learner writes Если он пришёл, мы бы поехали and leaves the если-clause looking like a real past condition. Russian puts бы in both clauses, and the first бы is the signal that the whole sentence is unreal. Spanish is closer, because si tuviera, iría marks both halves with a subjunctive and a conditional, so a Spanish speaker who notices the parallel acquires the double marking faster.

Two smaller patterns complete the system. Если бы не plus a noun means 'if it were not for': Если бы не дождь, мы бы пошли гулять (YEs-lee by ne dosht, my by pash-LEE goo-LYAT, 'if it were not for the rain, we would have gone for a walk'). And если is not the word for an indirect question. 'I do not know whether he will come' is Я не знаю, придёт ли он (ya ne ZNA-yoo, pree-DYOT lee on), with ли from lesson 102, never если.
lessons.example:
Read four conditions in a row and label each one before translating. General truth: Если много читать, слова запоминаются сами (YEs-lee MNO-ga chee-TAT, sla-VA za-pa-mee-NA-yoo-tsya, 'if you read a lot, words are remembered by themselves'). Future: Если поезд опоздает, мы не успеем на встречу (YEs-lee PO-yest a-paz-DA-yet, my ne oos-PYE-yem na FSTRYE-choo, 'if the train is late, we will not make the meeting'). Past real: Если он уже ушёл, звонить ему бессмысленно (YEs-lee on oo-ZHE oo-SHYOL, zva-NEET ye-MOO bees-SMYS-len-na, 'if he has already left, calling him is pointless'). Unreal: Если бы поезд не опоздал, мы бы успели (YEs-lee by PO-yest ne a-paz-DAL, my by oos-PYE-lee, 'if the train had not been late, we would have made it').

Now look at what changed between the second and fourth sentences. The second leaves the delay open: the train may be on time, and the speaker is planning for both outcomes. The fourth treats the delay as fact and the missed meeting as the consequence that did not happen. The verb in the если-clause went from опоздает to опоздал and gained бы, and the main clause went from не успеем to успели бы. Real conditionals leave the world open; unreal conditionals close it.

A paragraph can mix the two, and good writers do. Если мы подпишем договор в пятницу, работа начнётся в понедельник. Если бы мы подписали его в прошлом месяце, мы бы уже закончили первый этап. (YEs-lee my pad-PEE-shem da-ga-VOR f PYAT-nee-tsoo, ra-BO-ta nach-NYOT-sya f pa-nee-DYEL-neek. YEs-lee by my pad-pee-SA-lee ye-VO f PROSH-lam MYE-sya-tse, my by oo-ZHE za-KON-chee-lee PYER-vy ee-TAP.) 'If we sign the contract on Friday, the work begins on Monday. If we had signed it last month, we would already have finished the first stage.' The first sentence plans, the second reproaches, and the grammar marks the difference before a single evaluative word appears.
lessons.question: A colleague says «Если бы у нас было больше времени, мы бы проверили всё». You want to say the same thing about last week, when there was no time and the check did not happen. Does the sentence already say that, or does it need a different form?
lessons.answer: It already says it. The unreal conditional has one form for present, past and future, so the same sentence covers the missed check last week and a hypothetical shortage now; only context or a time adverb such as на прошлой неделе makes the past reading explicit.
lessons.distractor: It needs a past unreal form with a different ending in the main clause, because a sentence about last week cannot use the same verb form as a sentence about now.
lessons.correction: Adding an adverb is enough: Если бы у нас было больше времени, мы бы проверили всё на прошлой неделе. No ending changes, because Russian has no separate past unreal. What Cornell means when it says you need not worry about past, present or future is exactly this: the form проверили with бы serves every time reference, and the adverb or the context supplies the date. The distracter invents a tense distinction the language does not make, and it comes from English, where 'if we had had more time, we would have checked' is visibly different from 'if we had more time, we would check'. In Russian both readings are Если бы у нас было больше времени, мы бы проверили. What the learner must add is not a new ending but a time word when the context does not supply one.

depth.definitions: A real conditional presents the condition as open: it may hold or not, and the sentence says what follows if it does. An unreal conditional presents the condition as contrary to fact or as a pure hypothesis, and asserts nothing about whether it holds. The condition clause is the если-clause; the consequence clause is the main clause. Counterfactual is the special case of an unreal condition whose falsity the speaker knows, as in 'if I had known'. A conditional is not a tense but a relation between two clauses, which is why the same forms appear with past, present and future adverbs.
depth.mechanism:
Choose the type first, then the forms follow mechanically. For a real condition, put the verb of the если-clause in the tense and aspect the event requires: present for a general truth, perfective future for a single future event, past for a past condition. The main clause then takes whatever form its own meaning requires, which may be a future, a present, a past or an imperative. Nothing in the если-clause is marked as conditional; если is the only signal.

For an unreal condition, put бы after the verb in both clauses, or after the first stressed word of the clause, and put both verbs in the past form. The order of the clauses is free, and moving the condition to the end changes emphasis rather than meaning: Было бы плохо, если бы Саша не пришёл (BY-la by PLO-kha, YEs-lee by SA-sha ne pree-SHYOL, 'it would be bad if Sasha had not come'). When the condition is a noun rather than a clause, если бы не takes the nominative: Если бы не дождь.

The only form that needs care is the verb быть, because the past neuter было is the default for impersonal and weather conditions: Если бы было время, мы бы остались (YEs-lee by BY-la VRYE-mya, my by as-TA-lees). Do not agree было with время; the neuter is fixed in this construction, which is a small fossil worth learning as a phrase.
depth.secondExample:
Listen to a manager compare two plans, one open and one closed. Если мы возьмём кредит, мы сможем обновить оборудование (YEs-lee my vaz-MYOM kre-DEET, my SMO-zhem ab-na-VEET a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ye, 'if we take a loan, we will be able to renew the equipment'). Real, future, perfective in the condition, and the consequence is a future. Если бы мы взяли кредит в прошлом году, оборудование уже работало бы (YEs-lee by my VZYA-lee kre-DEET f PROSH-lam ga-DOO, a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ye oo-ZHE ra-BO-ta-la by, 'if we had taken a loan last year, the equipment would already be working'). Unreal, past reference, both verbs in the past form with бы.

Now add the objection that changes the register. Если бы не высокая ставка, мы бы давно это сделали (YEs-lee by ne vy-SO-ka-ya STAF-ka, my by dav-NO E-ta SDYE-la-lee, 'if it were not for the high rate, we would have done it long ago'). The condition is a noun phrase rather than a clause, and the pattern если бы не plus the nominative carries the whole counterfactual. A learner who tries Если бы не было высокой ставки is also grammatical, and it is heavier; both are correct, and the noun version is what a speaker reaches for in a meeting.
depth.mistake:
The most common error is a single бы, as in Если он пришёл, мы бы поехали. The sentence reads as a real condition with an unreal consequence, which is incoherent, and it comes straight from English, where 'would' appears only once. The repair is to say бы twice, once in each clause, until the pair is automatic: Если бы он пришёл, мы бы поехали.

The second error is the present tense after если бы, as in Если бы я знаю. бы cannot attach to a present-tense verb, because the past form is what supplies the event and бы supplies only the unreality. The repair is to change the verb, not to move бы: Если бы я знал.

The third error is using если for an embedded question. Я не знаю, если он придёт is a calque of 'I don't know if he will come'. Russian uses ли in that position, and если belongs to conditions: Я не знаю, придёт ли он. The same repair applies to 'whether' in reported questions, which lesson 76 already treated.
depth.application:
Write six sentences about your own plans, three real and three unreal, and say each pair aloud with the same content. For example: Если я закончу отчёт сегодня, я отправлю его вечером. Если бы я закончил отчёт вчера, я бы уже отправил его. (YEs-lee ya za-KON-choo at-CHYOT see-VO-dnya, ya at-PRAF-lyoo ye-VO VYE-chee-ram. YEs-lee by ya za-KON-cheel at-CHYOT fchee-RA, ya by oo-ZHE at-PRA-veel ye-VO, 'if I finish the report today, I will send it this evening. If I had finished the report yesterday, I would have sent it already.') Then change the time reference without changing the unreal forms: Если бы я закончил отчёт в прошлую пятницу, я бы уже отправил его. (YEs-lee by ya za-KON-cheel at-CHYOT f PROSH-loo-yoo PYAT-nee-tsoo, ya by oo-ZHE at-PRA-veel ye-VO, 'if I had finished the report last Friday, I would have sent it already.') The forms stay identical, and only the adverb moves.

Then read the six sentences to someone and ask them to say which are open and which are closed. If the listener hesitates, the бы is missing from one clause. This is the only reliable test, because the forms themselves are simple and the failure is always a missing marker rather than a wrong ending.
depth.summary: если plus ordinary indicative verbs makes a real condition, with the tense chosen by meaning and the perfective future used for a single future event. если бы plus the past form in both clauses makes an unreal condition, and one form covers present, past and future. English puts 'would' once, Russian puts бы twice, and the missing first бы is the error to listen for. Indirect questions take ли, not если.

lessons.title: Concession: хотя, несмотря на то что, and the obstacle that did not work
lessons.explanation:
A concessive clause names an obstacle and then says that the result happened anyway. The relationship is not cause and not contrast: the clause does not explain the result, it removes an explanation the hearer might have expected. Russian has two clause introducers for this, хотя (kha-TYA, 'although') and несмотря на то что (nee-smat-RYA na TO SHTO, 'despite the fact that'), plus a prepositional pattern for nouns, несмотря на plus the accusative. The choice between them is a choice of register and of what the obstacle is made of, and neither is a synonym for но.

хотя is the neutral, spoken and written introducer, and it takes an ordinary indicative verb in any tense. Хотя он устал, он продолжал работать (kha-TYA on oos-TAL, on pra-dal-ZHAL ra-BO-tat, 'although he was tired, he kept working'). The clause can also follow the main clause, where it sounds like an afterthought or a qualification: Он пришёл, хотя был занят (on pree-SHYOL, kha-TYA byl ZA-nyat, 'he came, although he was busy'). Moving the clause changes emphasis, not meaning, and it is the same positional logic as lesson 101: the fronted clause sets the background, the final clause adds a qualification to something already asserted.

In speech, хотя is very often paired with но in the main clause: Хотя он устал, но продолжал работать (kha-TYA on oos-TAL, no pra-dal-ZHAL ra-BO-tat). This double marking is common and entirely normal in conversation, and it is avoided in careful writing, where one marker is enough. A learner who writes it in a report will be understood and will sound conversational. The reverse error, omitting хотя and keeping но, produces a plain contrast rather than a concession, which is a different claim.

несмотря на то что is the bookish and journalistic version, and it presupposes the obstacle as a fact rather than presenting it as a possibility. Несмотря на то что шёл дождь, мы пошли гулять (nee-smat-RYA na TO SHTO shyol dosht, my pash-LEE goo-LYAT, 'despite the fact that it was raining, we went for a walk'). The difference from хотя is not truth or falsehood but weight: a news report, an official statement or an academic paragraph reaches for несмотря на то что, while a colleague in a corridor reaches for хотя. The comma comes before несмотря, because the whole group introduces the clause.

When the obstacle is a noun rather than a clause, the same meaning is carried by несмотря на plus the accusative, with no то что at all. Несмотря на дождь, мы пошли гулять (nee-smat-RYA na dosht, my pash-LEE goo-LYAT, 'despite the rain, we went for a walk'). Wiktionary's entry for несмотря на marks the government as accusative and gives a full example: Несмотря на серьёзную болезнь, наконец врачи вылечили меня (nee-smat-RYA na see-RYOS-noo-yoo ba-LYEZN, na-ka-NYETS vrah-CHEE VY-lee-chee-lee mee-NYA, 'despite a serious illness, the doctors finally cured me'). The noun phrase is short, which is why headlines and summaries prefer it.

Two related forms need separating. даже если (DA-zhe YEs-lee, 'even if') is a hypothetical concession: it grants a possibility, not a fact, and it therefore takes an ordinary conditional. Даже если он придёт, мы не изменим решение (DA-zhe YEs-lee on pree-DYOT, my ne eez-MYE-neem ree-SHYE-nee-ye, 'even if he comes, we will not change the decision'). хотя бы (kha-TYA by, 'at least') is not a conjunction at all: it is хотя plus the particle бы in a fixed adverbial meaning. Позвони хотя бы (paz-va-NEE kha-TYA by, 'at least call') has nothing to do with concession, and a learner who reads хотя бы as 'although' will misparse the sentence.
lessons.example:
Say the same content four ways and watch the register move while the meaning stays put. Spoken, clause first: Хотя переговоры затянулись, мы подписали договор (kha-TYA pee-ree-ga-VO-ry za-tee-noo-LEES, my pad-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR, 'although the negotiations dragged on, we signed the contract'). Spoken with the double marker: Хотя переговоры затянулись, но мы подписали договор. Written: Несмотря на то что переговоры затянулись, мы подписали договор. Headline style, noun phrase: Несмотря на затянувшиеся переговоры, договор подписан (nee-smat-RYA na za-tee-NOOF-shee-ye-sya pee-ree-ga-VO-ry, da-ga-VOR PAT-pee-san, 'despite the drawn-out negotiations, the contract has been signed').

Now change the relationship and listen to how the sentence stops being concessive. Потому что переговоры затянулись, мы подписали договор позднее (pa-ta-MOO SHTO pee-ree-ga-VO-ry za-tee-noo-LEES, my pad-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR POZD-nee-ye, 'because the negotiations dragged on, we signed the contract later') gives a cause. Переговоры затянулись, но мы подписали договор (pee-ree-ga-VO-ry za-tee-noo-LEES, no my pad-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR) gives a plain contrast with two equal claims. The concessive version does something narrower: it concedes the obstacle and still asserts the result, which is why it is the natural shape for a recommendation or a defence of a decision.

Add the hypothetical form to see the difference between fact and possibility. Даже если переговоры затянутся, мы подпишем договор в срок (DA-zhe YEs-lee pee-ree-ga-VO-ry za-tee-NOOT-sya, my pad-PEE-shem da-ga-VOR f srok, 'even if the negotiations drag on, we will sign the contract on time'). The negotiations have not dragged on yet, so the concession is about a future possibility, and the verb is a perfective future rather than a past fact.
lessons.question: You are writing a short report and produce «Несмотря на то что рост цен, спрос не снизился». What is wrong with it, and what are the two correct repairs?
lessons.answer: A clause introducer has been attached to a noun phrase. Either drop то что and use the preposition with the accusative, «Несмотря на рост цен, спрос не снизился», or keep the clause and give it a verb, «Несмотря на то что цены выросли, спрос не снизился».
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because несмотря на то что can introduce either a clause or a noun phrase, and the accusative рост цен is already correct after на.
lessons.correction: The accusative is indeed correct after на, which is exactly what makes the error hard to see: the case is right and the structure is wrong. несмотря на то что is a clause introducer and needs a subject and a verb after it; несмотря на is a preposition and takes a noun phrase. The distracter treats the two as one item with optional parts, but they are two different constructions that happen to share three words. This is a common slip in reports because the writer starts with the longer phrase and then writes a noun, and the repair costs one word either way: add a verb or delete то что.

depth.definitions: Concession is the relation in which an obstacle is acknowledged and the expected consequence does not follow. A concessive clause is the subordinate clause that names the obstacle. Presupposition is the treatment of something as already true rather than as newly asserted, which is what несмотря на то что does to its clause. Register is the level of formality a form belongs to, and хотя and несмотря на то что differ mainly in register rather than in truth conditions. A hypothetical concession grants a possibility with даже если, while a factual concession grants an established fact with хотя.
depth.mechanism:
Build the sentence from the two halves. First state the result you want to defend, then state the obstacle that would normally prevent it. Then choose the introducer by two criteria: is the obstacle a clause or a noun, and how formal is the text. A clause in speech takes хотя; a clause in a report takes несмотря на то что; a noun in any register takes несмотря на plus the accusative.

Placement follows the information rule from lesson 101. If the obstacle is already known or is being conceded before the main point, front it: Несмотря на то что цены выросли, спрос не снизился. If the obstacle is an afterthought or a qualification of a claim already made, put it last: Спрос не снизился, хотя цены выросли. Fronting the concession makes the sentence sound balanced and deliberate, which is why it dominates in editorials and reports. Putting it last makes the sentence sound like a correction, which is why it dominates in conversation.

The double marker хотя, но is a register decision, not a grammatical one. In speech it is normal and it adds emphasis to the main clause. In writing, choose one marker and drop the other, because the pair reads as spoken Russian transcribed.
depth.secondExample:
Read a paragraph from a market report and label the concession in each sentence. Несмотря на снижение ключевой ставки, банки не уменьшили проценты по кредитам (nee-smat-RYA na snee-ZHEE-nee-ye klyu-che-VOY STAF-kee, BAN-kee ne oo-MYEN-shee-lee pra-TSEN-ty pa kre-DEE-tam, 'despite the cut in the key rate, the banks did not reduce loan rates'). The obstacle is a noun phrase, so the prepositional pattern, and the result is the second clause. Хотя ставка снизилась ещё в сентябре, эффект оказался слабым (kha-TYA STAF-ka snee-ZEE-las yesh-SHYO f seen-teeb-RYE, eh-FYEKT a-ka-ZAL-sya SLA-bym, 'although the rate was cut back in September, the effect turned out to be weak'). The obstacle is now a clause and the register is slightly less formal, so хотя. Регулятор, несмотря на критику, сохранил курс (ree-goo-LYA-tar, nee-smat-RYA na knee-TEE-koo, sa-khra-NEEL koors, 'the regulator, despite the criticism, kept the rate').

Now note what the three sentences have in common: each one grants something that would normally push the result the other way, and then reports that the result held. That is the whole rhetorical job of concession, and it is why the pattern is so frequent in argument. A writer who uses но instead makes two claims of equal weight; a writer who uses хотя makes one claim and disarms an objection to it.
depth.mistake:
The first error is the mixed construction, несмотря на то что plus a noun, which the question above diagnoses. The repair is to decide whether the obstacle has a verb; if it does not, the preposition is несмотря на.

The second error is хотя бы read as 'although'. A learner sees хотя бы in a sentence and translates 'although', which produces nonsense, because хотя бы means 'at least' and belongs to requests and minimums: Скажи хотя бы слово (ska-ZHEE kha-TYA by SLO-va, 'say at least a word'). The repair is to check whether бы is present and whether the sentence is making a concession or asking for a minimum.

The third error is registering. A learner who has just learned несмотря на то что uses it in conversation and sounds like a communiqué, and a learner who writes reports with хотя sounds casual. Neither is grammatically wrong. The repair is to keep the pair as a register choice and to notice which one the text around you is using. A fourth error, common in Spanish speakers, is to calque aunque with the subjunctive and produce хотя бы он пришёл for 'although he came'; Russian concession takes the indicative, and the past form without бы is the correct one.
depth.application:
Take one decision you have made recently and write it three times: with хотя in a message to a colleague, with несмотря на то что in a paragraph of a report, and with несмотря на plus a noun in a heading. Read all three aloud and listen to how the same content changes its social temperature.

Then write two sentences that are not concessive but look similar, one with потому что and one with но, and check that you can say why each is different. Finish with a sentence that uses даже если about a risk that has not materialised, and one that uses хотя бы as a minimum. If you can produce all five without hesitating over the marker, the pattern is in place.
depth.summary: хотя introduces a factual concession in neutral register and takes the indicative; несмотря на то что does the same job in bookish and journalistic register; несмотря на plus the accusative does it for a noun. Concession grants an obstacle and asserts the result anyway, which is not the same as contrast with но. даже если grants a possibility, and хотя бы means 'at least' and is not a conjunction.

steps: Step 1, draw two boxes side by side. In the left box write ДОЖДЬ (dosht, rain) and label it 'obstacle'. In the right box write ПОШЛИ ГУЛЯТЬ (we went for a walk) and label it 'result'. The arrow between them runs against expectation, so draw it with a small barrier across it.
Step 2, write the clause version above the arrow: хотя шёл дождь. Mark it 'neutral register, clause'. Then write несмотря на то что шёл дождь below the arrow and mark it 'bookish register, clause'.

Step 3, replace the obstacle box with a noun phrase, ДОЖДЬ in the accusative, and write несмотря на дождь on the arrow. Mark it 'preposition, noun phrase'. Draw a cross through то что to show that the clause marker cannot stay.

Step 4, add a second arrow below, labelled даже если пойдёт дождь (DA-zhe YEs-lee pay-DYOT dosht, even if it rains), and mark it 'possibility, not fact'. This arrow starts from a dotted box, because the obstacle has not happened.
Step 5, add a margin note with хотя бы and a small circle around бы. Label it 'not a conjunction: at least'. This note sits outside the diagram because хотя бы does not express an obstacle at all.

lessons.title: Where the clause stands, and how to unpack a participle into one
lessons.explanation:
Two skills meet in this lesson, and they are the same skill seen from two sides. The first is placement: a Russian subordinate clause can stand before, after or inside the main clause, and the position is not free decoration, because it decides what the sentence presents as background and what it presents as news. The second is conversion: written Russian compresses clauses into participles and gerunds, spoken Russian expands them back into clauses, and a learner who can only read the compressed form is condemned to write it. Lesson 71 gave you the reading direction. This lesson gives you both directions and the register choice between them.

Begin with placement, because it governs everything else. The rule from lesson 101 still holds: new information goes last. A fronted subordinate clause is background, the thing the hearer is assumed to know or to be able to grant, and the main clause that follows carries the assertion. Compare Так как было поздно, мы ушли (TAK KAK BY-la POZ-na, my oosh-LEE, 'since it was late, we left') with Мы ушли, потому что было поздно (my oosh-LEE, pa-ta-MOO SHTO BY-la POZ-na, 'we left because it was late'). The first presents the lateness as shared ground and the departure as the point; the second presents the departure as known and the reason as the point. Both are grammatical, and they answer different questions.

A long fronted clause usually pulls a то into the main clause to mark the boundary. Если ты не против, то я пойду (YEs-lee ty ne PRO-teef, to ya pay-DOO, 'if you do not mind, I will go'). The то is not translatable and it is not obligatory, but it does real work: it tells the listener that the condition has ended and the consequence is starting, which matters when the condition contains its own commas. The same balancing то appears after когда, если and хотя, and it is one of the small signals that separates a controlled written sentence from a spoken one.

Now the conversion. Cornell's deverbals page states the equation that this whole lesson rests on: written style participles equal conversational style который clauses. The equation runs in both directions, and each direction has its own mechanics. A present active participle becomes который plus a present-tense verb: читающий книгу студент (chee-TA-yoo-shchee KNEE-goo stoo-DYENT, 'the student reading a book') becomes студент, который читает книгу (stoo-DYENT, ka-TO-ryy chee-TA-yet KNEE-goo). A past active participle becomes который plus a past-tense verb: компания, построившая завод (kam-PA-nee-ya, pa-STRO-eef-sha-ya za-VOT, 'the company that built the plant') becomes компания, которая построила завод. A past passive participle becomes который plus an active verb whose subject is the original agent, or an indefinite third-person plural when no agent is named: завод, построенный в 2019 году (za-VOT, pa-STRO-yen-nyy f DYE-vee-tsat dee-VYAT-na-tam ga-DOO, 'the plant built in 2019') becomes завод, который построили в 2019 году, and статья, написанная им (sta-TYA, na-PEE-san-na-ya eem, 'the article written by him') becomes статья, которую он написал.

Gerunds convert with conjunctions rather than with который, because they express circumstance rather than identity. An imperfective gerund names an action simultaneous with the main verb and becomes когда or пока plus an imperfective verb: читая газету, он ел (chee-TA-ya ga-ZYE-too, on yel, 'while reading the newspaper, he ate') becomes когда он читал газету, он ел. A perfective gerund names an action completed before the main verb and becomes после того как plus a perfective verb: прочитав отчёт, директор позвонил (pra-chee-TAF at-CHYOT, dee-RYEK-tar paz-va-NEEL, 'having read the report, the director called') becomes после того как директор прочитал отчёт, он позвонил.

Cornell's page on time clauses explains why the conjunction has to be a clause introducer rather than a preposition. Russian clauses are introduced by clause introducers, not by prepositions, so после обеда is a phrase and после того как он пообедал is a clause, and the four ways of saying one sequence are all available: Он пообедал и ушёл. После обеда он ушёл. После того как он пообедал, он ушёл. Пообедав, он ушёл. The last is the most compressed and the most written; the third is the most explicit; the first two are the most spoken.
lessons.example:
Take one sentence from a news report and unpack it twice. The report says Компания, построившая завод в 2019 году, планирует расширение (kam-PA-nee-ya, pa-STRO-eef-sha-ya za-VOT f DYE-vee-tsat dee-VYAT-na-tam ga-DOO, plan-EE-roo-yet ra-see-RYE-nee-ye, 'the company that built the plant in 2019 is planning an expansion'). Spoken version one, with который: Компания, которая построила завод в 2019 году, планирует расширение. Spoken version two, with the clause moved to the end: Компания планирует расширение, и построила она этот завод в 2019 году. The second is looser and more conversational, and it splits one sentence into two clauses joined by и, which is exactly what speech does when a written sentence becomes too dense.

Now a passive one, where the agent has to be recovered. Завод, построенный в 2019 году, выпускает удобрения (za-VOT, pa-STRO-yen-nyy f DYE-vee-tsat dee-VYAT-na-tam ga-DOO, vy-poo-ska-yet oo-da-BRYE-nee-ya, 'the plant built in 2019 produces fertiliser'). The participle has no agent, so the spoken version supplies an indefinite plural: Завод, который построили в 2019 году, выпускает удобрения. If the report does name the agent, the agent becomes the subject: Статья, написанная им, вызвала спор (sta-TYA, na-PEE-san-na-ya eem, VYZ-va-la spor, 'the article written by him caused a dispute') becomes Статья, которую он написал, вызвала спор.

Finally a gerund, which is where the subject test bites. Прочитав отчёт, директор позвонил is unambiguous because the director is the one who read and the one who called. Услышав новость, мы позвонили в офис (oos-LY-shav NO-vast, my paz-va-NEE-lee v OF-ees, 'having heard the news, we called the office') unpacks as После того как мы услышали новость, мы позвонили в офис. If you unpack it as После того как они услышали новость, мы позвонили, you have changed the subject and therefore changed the sentence, because the gerund never had a subject of its own.
lessons.question: You are preparing a spoken briefing from a written report that says «Решение, принятое советом директоров, вступает в силу в марте». How do you say it aloud without the participle, and what has to be decided in the process?
lessons.answer: «Решение, которое принял совет директоров, вступает в силу в марте». The participial phrase becomes a который clause, the agent совет директоров becomes the subject, and the passive short form вступает stays where it is because it is the main verb.
lessons.distractor: «Решение, которое принятое советом директоров, вступает в силу в марте», keeping the participle ending after который so that the passive meaning is preserved.
lessons.correction: Once который is there, the verb in the clause is a finite verb and cannot keep a participle ending. принятое is a participle agreeing with решение; принял is the finite past form agreeing with совет директоров, which is now the subject of the clause. The distracter doubles the marking, which is the single most common conversion error, because the learner feels that the passive meaning will be lost without the participle. It is not lost: который принял совет директоров says the same thing in the active voice, and Russian prefers that in speech. Note also that the short form вступает в силу is untouched, because the conversion only affects the compressed clause, not the main clause.

depth.definitions: A subordinate clause is a clause that fills a role inside a larger sentence, as subject, object, attribute or adverbial. Compression is the process of turning a clause into a phrase inside a noun phrase, which in Russian means a participle, or into an adverbial, which means a gerund. A participle is a verb form that declines like an adjective and modifies a noun. A gerund, in the Russian sense, is an indeclinable verb form that modifies the main verb and shares its subject. A correlative is a two-word introducer such as после того как or то, что, in which the first part declines and the second is fixed. Information structure is the division of a sentence into what is treated as known and what is asserted.
depth.mechanism:
Run the conversion as a table with four rows, one for each participle type, plus two rows for the gerunds. For an active present participle, the clause verb is present and the relative word is the subject: читающий becomes который читает. For an active past participle, the clause verb is past and the relative word is the subject: построившая becomes которая построила. For a passive present participle, the clause verb is present and the relative word is the object: обсуждаемый becomes который обсуждают. For a passive past participle, the clause verb is past and the relative word is the object: построенный becomes который построили, unless an agent is named, in which case the agent becomes the subject and the relative word becomes its object.

For gerunds, the row is chosen by aspect and by meaning. Imperfective plus simultaneous becomes когда or пока plus imperfective. Perfective plus prior becomes после того как plus perfective. A gerund that gives a reason becomes потому что or так как, and the test is whether the main clause answers 'why?' or 'when?'. In every row the tense is supplied by the participle's own shape, not by the main verb, which is why a present participle in a past sentence still becomes a present-tense clause.

Placement then applies to the result. Convert first, then decide whether the clause should stand where the participle stood, which keeps the original emphasis, or move to the end, which makes it the news. Converting without re-deciding the position produces a sentence that is grammatical and rhythmically wrong, because a participle sits inside a noun phrase and a clause wants room.
depth.secondExample:
Read the same paragraph in two registers and match the sentences one for one. Written: Отчёт, подготовленный аналитическим отделом, показывает рост, вызванный внутренним спросом (at-CHYOT, pad-ga-TOV-len-nyy a-na-lee-TEE-ches-keem at-DYE-lam, pa-KA-zy-va-yet roost, VYZ-van-nyy VNOOT-ren-neem SPRO-sam, 'the report prepared by the analytical department shows growth caused by domestic demand'). Spoken: Отчёт, который подготовил аналитический отдел, показывает, что внутренний спрос вызвал рост. Two conversions in one sentence, and the second one changes the syntax of the main clause as well, because вызванный is a participle inside a noun phrase while вызвал is a main verb with its own subject.

Written: Проанализировав данные, отдел пришёл к выводу, что спрос устойчив (pra-a-na-lee-zee-ro-VAF DAN-ny-ye, at-DYEL pree-SHYOL k VY-va-doo, SHTO spros oos-TOY-cheef, 'having analysed the data, the department concluded that demand is stable'). Spoken: После того как отдел проанализировал данные, он пришёл к выводу, что спрос устойчив. The gerund compressed a whole clause into one word and left the subject implicit; the spoken version has to say отдел twice, once as the subject of the first clause and once as the pronoun он.

What the pair shows is that compression saves words and costs explicitness. The written version is shorter and harder; the spoken version is longer and clearer. Neither is better in the abstract, and the skill is to know which one the situation wants.
depth.mistake:
The first error is the dangling gerund. A learner writes Прочитав отчёт, было принято решение, translating 'having read the report, a decision was made'. The gerund has no subject of its own, so it borrows the subject of the main clause, and the main clause here has no subject at all. The repair is to give the main clause a subject that can also do the reading: Прочитав отчёт, директор принял решение (pra-chee-TAF at-CHYOT, dee-RYEK-tar pree-NYAL ree-SHYE-nee-ye).

The second error is double marking, который plus a participle, as in который построенный. Once который is present, the verb is finite; the participle ending has to go. The repair is to choose the voice: который построил if the agent is the subject, который построили if the agent is unknown.

The third error is converting a prepositional phrase as if it were a clause. После обеда, он ушёл is fine as a phrase, but a learner who wants a clause writes после того как обед, producing a clause introducer with a noun. The repair is to add the verb: после того как он пообедал. The same trap appears with до того как, перед тем как and в то время как, all of which are correlatives and all of which need a clause.
depth.application:
Take a paragraph of written Russian from a report or a news item, about a hundred words, and rewrite it as speech: every participle becomes a который clause, every gerund becomes a когда, после того как or потому что clause. Read the spoken version aloud and check that each converted clause has a subject.

Then reverse the exercise on one sentence. Take your clearest spoken sentence and compress it, keeping only the main clause and turning one subordinate clause into a participle. Compare the two versions for length and for difficulty, and notice which one you would say to a colleague and which one you would put in a report.

Finish by moving one clause from the front to the end of its sentence and saying what changed. If nothing changed in your reading, the emphasis was not being carried by position, and the sentence probably needs a different order.
depth.summary: Fronted clauses are background and final clauses are news, and то often marks the boundary in a long sentence. Written participles equal spoken который clauses, and the conversion changes the verb from a participle to a finite form. Gerunds become когда, после того как or потому что clauses, and the subject of the gerund is the subject of the main clause, which is why the conversion has to restore a subject. Choose the register first, then convert.

readings.note: Read the whole page, which is a single paragraph and one displayed equation: written style participles equal conversational style который clauses. It also notes which deverbal forms do occur in conversation, the short past passive participles and the present deverbal adverbs, so the equation is not absolute and the exceptions are named. Caveat: the Cyrillic is in a legacy font and arrives garbled, and the page is a summary that assumes you have read the four participle pages and the two gerund pages.

It also states the reason the conjunction cannot be replaced by a preposition: Russian clauses are introduced by clause introducers, not by prepositions. That is the grammatical fact behind the whole conversion exercise. Caveat: same encoding problem, and the page belongs to the last lessons of the Cornell sequence, so its examples are long.

The page shows the imperfective gerund in -я, spelled -а after ч, щ, ш and ж, and the way it names an action simultaneous with the main verb, which is the row of the conversion table that becomes когда plus an imperfective. It also notes that some imperfective verbs have no present gerund at all, so the form is recognised rather than derived on demand, and it lists the fixed expressions честно говоря (CHEST-na ga-va-RYA, 'frankly speaking') and не говоря уже о Москве (ne ga-va-RYA oo-ZHE a mask-VYE, 'to say nothing of Moscow'). visual.description: A labelled text diagram: a two-column table with six rows, the left column holding the compressed form and the right column holding the expanded clause, plus a register arrow across the top. Rendered as text steps, not as an image.

Step 2, fill the first four rows with the participles: читающий against который читает, построившая against которая построила, обсуждаемый against который обсуждают, построенный against который построили. Beside each pair write the voice and the tense, because those are what the conversion preserves.

Step 3, fill the last two rows with the gerunds: читая газету against когда он читал газету, and прочитав отчёт against после того как он прочитал отчёт. Mark the first as simultaneous and the second as prior.

Step 4, add a column on the right for the subject of the clause. Every row must have one, and the gerund rows are the ones where the learner forgets it. Write 'no subject of its own' beside the gerund forms and draw an arrow from the main clause subject into the empty slot.

Step 5, add a footer note with the placement rule: compressed forms sit inside a noun phrase, expanded clauses can move, and a clause moved to the end becomes the news. This note connects the table to the first half of the lesson.

questions.prompt: You are introducing a new colleague and want to say 'here is the person I work with'. Which completion of «Вот человек, ___ я работаю» is correct?
questions.correction: работать с кем, 'to work with someone', takes the instrumental, so the relative word is которым and the preposition с stands immediately in front of it: Вот человек, с которым я работаю (vot chee-la-VYEK, s ka-TO-rym ya ra-BO-ta-yoo). The distracter keeps который in the nominative because it agrees with человек in gender and number, which is only half of the rule from lesson 111; the case is decided inside the clause.

questions.prompt: A manager writes «Я хочу, ___ вы проверили цифры до пятницы». Which conjunction belongs in the gap?
questions.correction: хотеть expresses a wish, not a report, and the two verbs have different subjects, so the conjunction is чтобы and the dependent verb takes the past form: Я хочу, чтобы вы проверили цифры (ya kha-CHOO, SHTO-by vy pra-VYE-ree-lee TSEEF-ry). The past form does not mean past time; Friday has not arrived yet. The distracter reports a fact, which would make the sentence mean 'I want that you checked', a claim about the world rather than a request.

questions.prompt: Which sentence says 'if the train had not been late, we would have made the meeting'?
questions.answer: Если бы поезд не опоздал, мы бы успели.
questions.distractor: Если поезд не опоздал, мы бы успели.
questions.correction: An unreal condition puts бы in both clauses, because the first бы is what marks the whole sentence as contrary to fact: Если бы поезд не опоздал, мы бы успели (YEs-lee by PO-yest ne a-paz-DAL, my by oos-PYE-lee). The distracter puts бы only in the main clause, which is the English pattern of a single 'would', and it leaves the если-clause reading as a real past condition. English and Spanish speakers both make this error, and the repair is to say бы twice.

questions.prompt: You are writing a paragraph of a formal report and need to concede that prices rose while demand did not fall. Which sentence fits the register?
questions.answer: Несмотря на то что цены выросли, спрос не снизился.
questions.distractor: Хотя цены выросли, но спрос не снизился.
questions.correction: The second sentence is grammatical and belongs to speech, where хотя is often paired with но for emphasis. A report takes the bookish clause introducer несмотря на то что and one marker only: Несмотря на то что цены выросли, спрос не снизился (nee-smat-RYA na TO SHTO TSE-ny VY-ros-lee, spros ne SNEE-zee-sya). The distracter is not wrong Russian; it is the wrong register, which is exactly the distinction lesson 114 draws.

questions.prompt: A written report says «Решение, принятое советом директоров, вступает в силу в марте». Which is the correct spoken version?
questions.answer: Решение, которое принял совет директоров, вступает в силу в марте.
questions.distractor: Решение, которое принятое советом директоров, вступает в силу в марте.
questions.correction: Converting a past passive participle means turning the agent into the subject of a который clause: принятое советом директоров becomes которое принял совет директоров, with a finite past verb. The distracter keeps the participle ending after который, which is double marking and is ungrammatical, because a который clause needs a finite verb. The main clause is untouched, since the conversion only affects the compressed phrase.
